title: LinkedIn Content Coaching vs. Ghostwriting: Who Writes the Posts?
summary: Should you hire a LinkedIn coach or a ghostwriter? Compare who writes the posts, what stays on your plate, and how to test the right fit for your team.
body_markdown:
A LinkedIn content coach helps you get better at writing your own posts. A LinkedIn ghostwriter turns your ideas into drafts you can review. For a founder deciding between the two, the quickest test is to look at the last three posts you meant to publish. Where did they stop?


If you wrote drafts but couldn’t tell which ones were worth sharing, start with coaching. If the ideas never made it out of voice notes or Slack messages, start with ghostwriting. And if good drafts are already sitting in review, fix the approval step before buying either service.


What happens each week? LinkedIn content coaching LinkedIn ghostwriting


Who writes the first draft? You or someone on your team. The writer, using your interviews, notes, or examples.


What do you do? Write, revise, and put the feedback into practice. Share what happened, check the draft for accuracy and voice, and approve it.


What should improve? You get better at spotting a post idea and turning it into a draft. More of the ideas you already have reach review as complete drafts.


Editing, scheduling, and engagement depend on the scope. Ask who owns each one rather than assuming it comes with the service.


## Choose coaching if you want to keep writing


Coaching is useful when you enjoy writing and can protect time for it, but your drafts tend to read like product updates or internal memos. A coach can help you find the part an outside reader would care about and show you what to cut.


Say you finish a draft about a new reporting feature. The draft starts with the launch date and walks through the interface. In a coaching session, you might realize the interesting part is why customers kept exporting the old report to a spreadsheet. You rewrite the post around that behavior and the decision it led to. The next time you have a release to talk about, you know what to look for.


The test is what happens when the coach isn’t in the room. Can you make a similar change on the next draft without waiting for someone to point it out? If so, you’re getting something you can reuse.


## Choose ghostwriting if the first draft keeps slipping


Ghostwriting makes more sense when you can explain a useful idea in conversation, but writing keeps losing to the rest of your job. Give the writer one specific decision: what your team assumed, what you saw, and what you changed. That is more useful than asking for a post about “our approach to reporting.”


You still need time for review. For a technical founder, that often means catching a sentence that sounds good but says more than the evidence supports. If a customer exported one report to fix a single handoff, don’t let the draft imply that every customer does it. A good writer should be able to revise the claim without losing the point.


If you’re evaluating a writer, use a real source excerpt you can share and compare it with the draft. Rethoric’s[guide to evaluating a LinkedIn ghostwriter’s writing sample](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/evaluate-linkedin-ghostwriter-writing-sample) shows what to check before you commit.


## Test one week of work before you choose


Pick two ideas from conversations you already had. Write down who the posts are for and which details are safe to share. Then try the arrangement that matches the bottleneck:


- **Coaching:** Bring one rough draft to a session. Revise it from the feedback, then write the second post on your own. See whether the feedback helped you make the second draft stronger.
- **Ghostwriting:** Give the writer the same kind of raw notes you can produce during a busy week. Ask for one draft and a revision. See how much new work you do in review and whether the revised post still sounds like you.


Track who owns the next step and how long it sits with them. A good draft that stays in review for ten days tells you something about your workflow, not just your choice of writer. If an internal teammate already writes well, you may only need outside editing or a writer for interview-led pieces. Rethoric’s[guide to building a LinkedIn content team](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/linkedin-content-team-for-founders) covers how to split that work.


## Frequently asked questions


### Can a LinkedIn coach edit my drafts?


Yes, if editing is included in the agreement. Ask whether the coach will suggest changes, do a line edit, or rewrite sections. Those leave you with different amounts of work.


### Do I still need to review posts a ghostwriter writes?


Yes. You know which claims are accurate, which details are private, and whether you’d stand behind the point in public. Assign someone else to check product or customer details when necessary, but keep final approval clear.


### Can I use both coaching and ghostwriting?


Yes. You might keep writing quick reactions yourself and have a ghostwriter handle posts that need interviews or more editing. Set the split before you start so both people aren’t working on the same draft.
